svg.title: Battery types compared
svg.desc: A comparison of five rechargeable battery types, one row each, with the volts per cell, a bar for energy per kilogram on a 0 to 300 watt-hours per kilogram scale, what each is mostly used for, and one thing to watch out for. Lead-acid (AGM), highlighted green because it is the one the FRC robot must use (rule R601): 2.0 V per cell (2.1 V full), 35 to 40 Wh/kg; used for the FRC robot, car starting and backup power; a short can arc over 500 A, so insulate the terminals (R607). Nickel-cadmium (NiCd): 1.2 V per cell, 40 to 60 Wh/kg; used for power tools and emergency lights, and its cousin NiMH (1.2 V, no cadmium) powers FTC robots; cadmium is toxic so recycle it, and it suffers from memory. Lithium polymer (LiPo): 3.7 V per cell (4.2 V full), 100 to 265 Wh/kg; used for drones and RC models (3S is 11.1 V) and thin phones and tablets; a puncture, overcharge or over-discharge can make it swell and burn. Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4, LiFe): 3.2 V per cell (3.65 V full), 95 to 172 Wh/kg; used for solar and RV storage, and 4 cells (12.8 V) can replace a 12 V lead-acid battery; the safest lithium type but it still needs a battery management system. Lithium-ion (Li-ion): 3.6 V per cell (4.2 V full), 160 to 300 Wh/kg; used for laptops such as the Driver Station, phones, power tools and electric cars; never float-charge it, and a damaged or overcharged cell can catch fire. A note explains that each lithium cell must stay inside its voltage window and cells in a series pack drift apart, so a battery management system balances them and cuts off the charge. A box lists the 2026 FRC rules: R601, exactly 1 sealed lead-acid battery, 12 V and 17 to 18.2 Ah, runs the robot; R602, other batteries only for COTS computers and cameras, either USB packs of 100 Wh or less or batteries built into the device; R605, no other batteries on the robot, not even as ballast. Our MK ES17-12 holds 12 V times 18 Ah, 216 Wh, in 5.86 kg: about 37 Wh/kg. Sources: Wikipedia infoboxes for energy per kilogram, Battery University for cell volts, the MK ES17-12 datasheet, WPILib and the 2026 FRC game manual.

g.text: Why lithium needs a BMS: every cell must stay inside its voltage window
(Li-ion: 4.2 V max), and cells in a series pack drift apart. A battery management
system balances them and cuts off the charge. Lead-acid takes a gentle float.

svg.text: On the FRC robot (2026 game manual)

g.text: R601: exactly 1 sealed lead-acid battery runs the robot: 12 V, 17 to 18.2 Ah.
R602: other batteries only for COTS computers and cameras: USB packs
of 100 Wh or less, or batteries built into the device (a laptop, a GoPro).
R605: no other batteries on the robot, not even as ballast.
